title: The intention to fast
hookLine: the intention for Ramadan, made each night or once for the month, by school

cards: Skip breakfast and lunch, and by afternoon the body can't tell why. Too busy to eat? Or fasting?
Same empty stomach, same slump, same glance at the clock. The difference is invisible, and it happened before the day began: someone decided.
The Islamic fast begins not at dawn with the first hunger but earlier, in the mind, with a word the legal books set at the start of acts of worship. Today, the intention to fast.

teach.b: First, the command. Surah two, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil)."
The fast has a purpose, and a purpose needs someone who means it. Second, the word is niyyah, intention.

The collection of Imam al-Bukhari opens with a saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: actions are judged by intentions, and each person gets what they intended. That's why a forgotten lunch and a fast aren't the same.
A report in the Sunan of Abu Dawud and others ties this to fasting: whoever doesn't resolve to fast before dawn has no fast. Third, how often? Here the schools differ.

teach.h: EACH NIGHT, OR ONCE: BY SCHOOL.
teach.b: Some, such as the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools, teach that the intention for each obligatory day of Ramadan is made each night, before dawn.
The Maliki school holds that one intention at the start of the month can cover it all, as long as the fast isn't broken off.

The Hanafi school allows a Ramadan day's intention later, before about the middle of the day, if nothing has been eaten. Shia jurists have their own rulings too. Each school has its reasons, and Muslims follow their own.

teach.h: IN THE HEART, NOT THE TONGUE.
teach.b: The jurists place it in the heart, not on the tongue; some count waking for the pre-dawn meal as a sign of it.
Some say a spoken intention helps focus the mind; others think saying it aloud isn't needed. And the lesson travels: the same act can be two different things, depending on what you meant by it.

how: Muslims make the intention to fast in the heart before dawn; Shafi'i and Hanbali Muslims renew it each night of Ramadan, Malikis may make one intention for the month, and Hanafis may make it until around midday for a Ramadan fast.

practice: Pick one thing you'll do tomorrow without thinking, a meal, a commute, a meeting, a call to your mother, and decide now what it's for, not what you'll get out of it. Hold that one sentence in your mind.
If you're planning a fast, you can make its intention tonight, in the way your school teaches.

wordCard.voice: The intention to fast. Niyyah: resolving in the heart, before dawn, to fast for Allah; each night or once for the month, depending on the school. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: intention, the resolve in the heart that makes an act worship.

carryVoice: Your line: intend it. The fast begins in the heart, before the first hunger. Until tomorrow.
